4131.prule: Fixed word-final stress: every word has a strong (full) syllable in the ultimate position and the stress falls on it; the penultimate syllable is unstressed and is where reduced weak syllables (vowel /ə/, short, assimilating to the following vowel) occur. No weight or vowel-quality condition is stated; the reduction is presented as a consequence of the unstressed position (taA- becomes təA- before a stressed strong syllable), not as a trigger of stress.
4131.srule: Antepenultimate syllables 'can take a stress before an unstressed penultimate syllable' (in addition to the fixed final stress): a trisyllabic phonological word is [stressable antepenult] + unstressed penult + stressed ultimate, shown by taA- keeping full /a/ there (ex. 4 taA- suBsuB 'something warm', taA- qoAʔʮæA 'something sweet'; taA- muA- ntoɴC ex. 6). Not labelled 'secondary', not ranked against the final stress, hedged ('suggest', 'can'); no words over three syllables discussed.

At the phonetic level, however, in final syllables the registers are realised as six allotones in complementary distribution according to the nature of the syllable final. ... phonologically significant tones at present belong to the peripheral system of the language and are completely absent from its core system.

4138.tone: Tone language: two underlying tones H and L per the LLBA abstract of Andersen 1992 ('pitch contrasts are analyzed in terms of two underlying tones, high & low'; saved excerpt file), three level tones plus contours per Gilley 2004 and PHOIBLE 1316; Storch 2005 sec. 5.2.2 fragments show tone alternations in noun inflection ('a low tone becomes a falling tone and a high or falling tone becomes low' in the oblique). On stress Storch says only that in Burun it 'has no grammatical or lexical function' and that it 'did not exist in Burun'; no source opened places stress on any syllable. 4145.prule: Primary word stress falls in a right-edge three-syllable window: penultimate by default; antepenultimate in lexical items whose final syllable is one of the 'weak final syllables', which in the western and southwestern dialects (the group in which Howe places Mahafaly and Tandroy, with Tanalana added after Dahl 1952) are -ke, -tse (Howe 2017: 48 after Dahl 1952); a small number of words have final-syllable stress. The position is decided by the segmental shape of the final syllable, not by syllable count or weight. The penultimate default is stated for Malagasy as a whole; the -ke/-tse clause is stated for the western and southwestern dialects as a group, not for Mahafaly by name. Adelaar 2019's two stress-marked Mahafaly forms fit it: tùmbukĕ 'foot' (antepenult before weak -kĕ) and rànju (penult).

[...] A word can thus have different syllables stressed in different contexts. There appear to be also other factors involved in stress assignment in …
4152.dloc: Huber 2011, Ch. 2 Phonology, section 2.6.2 'Stress in the utterance', p. 93; contrast section 2.6, p. 87
4152.heavy: The defining feature of heavy syllables is that they consist of two morae (p. 90): syllables with a diphthong (kamunei, dada-uai) or a long vowel (leteroo, sotemee). Closed syllables are not heavy in Huber's account (asan [ˈʔasan] 'long' stressed on the penult, p. 92). Fogaça 2015 (Makasae proper) additionally counts a final CVC with glottal-stop coda as heavy: 'quando a última sílaba é considerada pesada, o acento recai sobre ela, sendo assim classificado como sensível à quantidade (SQ). Nestes casos a formação do peso silábico ocorre por meio de ocorrências do tipo CVC ou CV, sendo V sempre alongada' (p. 82; examples fila', ira', apaa, asawaa); conclusion p. 164: 'quando a última sílaba é considerada pesada, ela atrai o acento para si'.
4152.dflt: penultimate syllable (all-light words: 10 010 0010; quadrisyllables carry initial secondary stress, [ˌisaˈrami])
4152.prule: Main stress on the head of the rightmost moraic trochee, feet built right to left: on the penultimate syllable when the final syllable is light (fala, lolitu, isarami; disyllabic grammatical items ani, =na'a, =fata), on the final syllable when it is heavy, i.e. bimoraic with a long vowel or diphthong (kamunei, dada-uai, leteroo, sotemee). A coda consonant adds no weight (asan ['ʔasan] penult-stressed); an odd initial light mora is stranded (lolitu). Echo vowels count as morae and shift stress ([a'sa:na]).
4152.srule: Secondary stress on the first syllable of lexical items in which more than one syllable precedes the main stress ([ˌisaˈrami], [ˌusuˈpadu], [ˌɾaɾaˈnini]; heavy-final [ˌkamuˈnɛi], [ˌlɛtɛˈrɔː]), giving a trochaic rhythm (left-headed bimoraic feet built right to left, main stress on the last foot, other foot heads secondary); an initial heavy (long-vowel) syllable forms its own foot and carries a secondary, near-equal stress ([ˌmiːˈtini] mit=ini, [ˌpuːˈlata] 'head', [ˌsɔːˈkɔɾɔˈkɔɾɔ] 'snore', loans [ˌviːˈtima], [ˌsaːˈpatu]). A single light syllable before the main stress is unstressed (lolitu [lɔˈlitu]).

4153.dq: 有些字如語助詞，及複合詞之前一個字，及一句中意義不重的字皆可輕讀。 (word-level: the first member of a compound word; sentence-level: particles and words of little semantic weight in a sentence -- one rule for both)
4153.dloc: p.7, section (二)音韵, 5.聲調 first sentence and the whole of 6.輕聲; supporting p.6 §3 元音 (4) and §4 韵母; identity p.2 序 and (一)導論.
4153.prule: No word-stress rule. Mak has seven lexical tones (one rare, mostly in recent Chinese loans). Prominence is described only as destressing (輕讀 'light reading' / 輕聲): grammatical particles, the first syllable of a compound word, and semantically light words in a sentence may be read light, in which case the syllable loses its lexical tone and takes a neutral half-high (raised dot) or half-low (low dot) pitch with the short central vowel ə; a weaker 'half-light' grade (半輕讀) keeps the tone with lowered, compressed pitch. Light vs. heavy reading of such words is mostly optional (輕重兩可).
4153.srule: Not mentioned in Li 1948 ((二)音韵 §5 聲調-§6 輕聲, p.7; §§3-4, p.6; TOC p.1 read): the sketch gives no stress rule and no secondary stress; its only prominence statement is the optional destressing (輕讀 / 半輕讀) already in the primary field.
4153.quote: 5. 聲調：莫話共有七個聲調，其中一個少見，且多在借字中出現。[...] (7) 高平調：略如北平的陰平。此調少見，多是漢語近來借字 [...]。 6. 輕聲：有些字如語助詞，及複合詞之前一個字，及一句中意義不重的字皆可輕讀。輕讀時有兩個調 (1) 半高，在字前加高點，如 ˙tə k'un 路上，˙ti ka:u 原處，(2) 半低，在字前加低點，如 .tə ma 馬，.lə ʐa:u 女婿。有些字讀時雖輕，但仍不失其原來聲調，只音調低些及音程縮小而已，這可以叫作半輕讀。這類字除字前加低點外，後仍附調號，如 ma .ʔe. pa:i lun na ˙li 我媽上舅舅家去了。這類字多輕重兩可。本篇材料收集時說話相當的慢，因此也許有許多輕讀的字變成半輕讀了。 [p.6, §3 元音 (4)] 短 ə 是央元音，又為輕讀之元音 [...] [p.6, §4 韵母:] 短元音單獨不成韵母（除因輕讀而短者外）

4153.tone: Seven lexical tones listed with Chao letters and Chinese-dialect comparisons on p.7: (1) 低升調 low rising, (2) 低降調 low falling, (3) 半高平調 mid-high level, (4) 全降調 full falling, (5) 高升調 high rising, (6) 中升調 mid rising, (7) 高平調 high level (rare, mostly recent Chinese loans, e.g. kwa:ŋ 廣, la:u 老). Stress/accent is treated only under 6.輕聲: light (destressed) syllables lose tone and take one of two neutral pitches (half-high ˙, half-low.), 'half-light' syllables keep tone with lowered, compressed pitch; the light syllables cited are prefix-like presyllables of compounds (˙tə k'un, ˙ti ka:u.tə ma.lə ʐa:u) and sentence particles (.ʔe, ˙li). No positive stress position (initial/final) is ever asserted.

(2) 低降調 low falling 'from mid to low' (lu:ŋ 銅)
(3) 半高平調 half-high level 'level between high and mid' (ʔdai 得)
(4) 全降調 full falling 'from high to low' (la:k 子)

tn.quote: 5. 聲調：莫話共有七個聲調，其中一個少見，且多在借字中出現。(1) 低升調 ... 由低升至中調，略似北平上聲 ... (2) 低降調 ... 由中調降到低 ... (3) 半高平調 ... 爲高中之間的平調，似廣州的陰去 ... (4) 全降調 ... 由高降到低，似廣州陰平(單字音) ... (5) 高升調 ... 由中升到高，似廣州陰上 ... (6) 中升調 ... 由半低起時保持平度至相當的時間然後微升，有時候感覺幾乎是半低平調 ... (7) 高平調 ... 略如北平的陰平。此調少見，多是漢語近來借字，例 kwa:ŋ (廣), la:u (老) 等
tn.translation: 5. Tones: Mak has seven tones in all; one is rare and occurs mostly in loanwords. (1) low rising: low to mid, rather like the Peiping shang tone ... (2) low falling: mid to low ... (3) half-high level: level between high and mid, like Cantonese yin-qu ... (4) full falling: high to low, like Cantonese yin-ping (citation form) ... (5) high rising: mid to high, like Cantonese yin-shang ... (6) mid rising: starts half-low, stays level a while, then rises slightly; at times almost a half-low level tone ... (7) high level: like Peiping yin-ping; rare, mostly recent Chinese loans, e.g. kwa:ŋ, la:u.
tn.cite: Li Fang-kuei 李方桂. 1948. 莫話記略 (Notes on Mak Language). Bulletin of the Institute of History and Philology, Academia Sinica 19: 1-80.

tn.note: Seven syllable tones (two level, five contour; the high level is rare, mostly Chinese loans). Checked -p/-t/-k syllables take 4 of them by vowel length. Light-read (destressed) syllables lose tone.

Woodward 1923-1926 (Ruvuma/Masasi Makua, open text read) has no accent statement in its alphabet section (pp. 270-271: 'These vowels occur short or long, just as in Swahili and other Bantu languages') and only two tense-distinguishing prominence remarks: p. 290 §35 'The a of the third person singular (being really aa) has a stress which distinguishes it from the previous tense. In that tense the -ho- is emphasized.' and p. 292 §43 'The first syllable is stressed, and this distinguishes it from the relative.' — these are prefix-H-tone contrasts in Kisseberth's terms (p. 553: 'some prefixes have a H tone associated with them in specific morphological constructions'), not a word-stress rule. van der Wal 2009: 20, 34 (Enahara variant, not Meetto) states Makhuwa lacks automatic penultimate lengthening.

Philippson 1991 (thesis, DDL PDF, saved excerpt pp. 399, 440-441, 507-508) calls Imitthupi Makua 'langue purement accentuelle' and speaks of 'accent sur le préfixe ou accent sur l'initiale du thème' with -ana taking 'l'accent par défaut (sur la pénultième)' — this is his pitch-accent analysis of where the H tone docks (data from Tanzanian Imitthupi; footnote on Esaaka), not a demarcative word stress; his annex lists no demarcative penultimate accent for Makua. Sacramento 1906 'Accentuação' nos. 7-13 (re-read) uses accent marks for open/closed vowel quality and gives no stress position.
